Le 19 octobre 2023, les gouvernements Le: On October 19, 2023, the Legault and Trudeau governments announced joint, equally shared investments of $1.8 billion for the construction of social and affordable housing in the Belle Province.
À Montréal, dans le quartier Saint-Miche: In Montréal's Saint-Michel neighbourhood, the news coincides with the creation of a housing committee. A group of community workers and volunteers has received it with optimism, but also with apprehension. The neighbourhood, a gateway for many newcomers and young families living below the poverty line, is hit hard by the shortage of affordable housing.
La Converse a parcouru les rues de ce qu: La Converse walked the streets of this neighbourhood in the east end of the city to listen and gather the words of the tenants who live there.
<strong>« Maintenant, on ne cherche plus: “Now, we're not looking for the right place anymore, we're just looking for a roof!”
Sous une tente plantée à l’entrée du Caf: Under a tent set up at the entrance of Café Saint-Mich, it's cigarette break time for Redouane. After a workday spent criss-crossing the streets of Montréal, the taxi driver waits patiently for his buddies in the dim light of the falling night. A cigarette in one hand, an espresso in the other, Redouane is unstoppable when it comes to talking about how hard it is to find affordable housing, in Saint-Michel as elsewhere on the island.
Le Café Saint-Mich est le repère de nomb: Café Saint-Mich is an evening haunt for many workers, including Redouane and Mohamed.
Il arrive du Maroc en 2018 avec la tête: He arrived from Morocco in 2018 with his head full of dreams, but his honeymoon with the province ended with the sudden rise in rents and the cost of living. A manager in his native country and holder of a master's degree in management, Redouane dropped everything with his wife to live the Quebec adventure. Today, he says he is disappointed and has realized that the promise of a new life was only a mirage. “Everything is expensive! All I'm asking for is some stability so I can live. Just that. To live well. But it's become impossible.”
Père de quatre enfants âgés de 3 à 11 an: A father of four children aged 3 to 11, he describes how gruelling his recent search for housing for himself and his family was. “It was a real ordeal! Landlords asked me to provide my credit history; I barely use my card. They also asked how many kids I have, when they're not even allowed to. I was stressed right until the end. They'd rather rent a 5 ½ to a family of three than to a family like mine.”
Heureusement, Redouane réussit à la dern: Fortunately, at the last minute, Redouane managed to find a place in public housing (HLM) in Montréal-Nord. But the good luck quickly gave way to disillusion. Appalled by the condition of the unit, but with no alternative, he moved in anyway. “It's an apartment that's been very poorly maintained, very poorly insulated. Heating costs me $253 a month. It's indecent! Our apartment is in the basement, and some of the bedroom windows are blocked; that's fewer emergency exits for us! It's not safe. (...) Now, we're not looking for the right place anymore, we're just looking for a roof!” he exclaims. Though Redouane's face seems to show great weariness, the man is not done speaking his mind.
Jusque-là silencieux, Mohamed, un compat: Until now silent, Mohamed, a fellow countryman and friend of Redouane's, nods his head as he draws on his cigarette. The man in his sixties, who has lived in Saint-Michel for eight years, also has plenty to say. “Two years ago, our landlord asked my wife and me to leave the apartment where we lived so he could move his son in, who had apparently just gotten married. We had no way of verifying it, but we had to leave anyway. Luckily, we managed to find something affordable fairly quickly. It came at the right time. Now I'm looking for an apartment for my daughter, who is arriving soon from Morocco. It's pure madness. The other day, I saw a 4 ½ for $1,400 on Champdoré Street. Before, you would never have seen that in Saint-Michel!”
Pour Redouane et Mohamed, il est impossi: For Redouane and Mohamed, it is impossible to stand up to landlords who throw their weight around and take advantage of the vulnerability of fragile tenants. “It's not up to me to investigate what landlords claim. That's not my role!” Mohamed points out. His friend picks up: “Where is the government in this war between landlords and tenants? We have to find a solution.”
Dans les salons de coiffure et les resta: In the hair salons and restaurants along Saint-Michel Boulevard, conversations come back to much the same words, the same rumours, the same grievances. Here, people fear having to leave their neighbourhood and move farther north; there, they are terrified at the thought of having to sacrifice more money for housing. Then there's the price of groceries, on everyone's lips, along with the constant wish to simply live in peace, at home.
Le restaurant la Belle Anne est un incon: The restaurant La Belle Anne is a must-visit, where a few people gather in the small dining room.
<strong>« La création d’un comité de log: “Creating a housing committee (...) is a starting point”
Dans les locaux du Forum Jeunesse de Sai: In the offices of the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel (FJSM), on the evening of October 25, about twenty people have gathered to mark the birth of an organization that many residents have long hoped for. On the menu: small bites and fruity drinks. Most of those present are community workers and residents of the neighbourhood. People are happy to be together with fellow fighters, and conversations are lively.
Après plusieurs années de travail, on y: After several years of work, they've finally made it. Before that, they had to face the administration, the paperwork, the bureaucracy and its endless hassles. But today it's official: the Comité Logement Citoyen Saint-Michel has come to life in front of a rather proud gathering. A few photos are taken to immortalize this important moment.
Désormais, il y aura dans le quartier un: From now on, the neighbourhood will have an organization that defends tenants' rights. In addition to offering individual support and information to residents, the Comité Logement Citoyen Saint-Michel will carry out social mobilization, popular education and advocacy, with the interests of the most disadvantaged at the heart of its mission.
Membre fondateur du comité et natif du q: A founding member of the committee and a Saint-Michel native, Alexandre Boucher Bonneau knows the hardest part is just beginning. “Creating a housing committee won't solve everything, it's a starting point. It will be a gathering place for all residents.” With the gentrification likely to accompany the extension of the Blue Line, the arrival of the BRT on Pie-IX Boulevard (bus rapid transit service, editor's note) and the condo towers sprouting up all around, he expects the pressure on the most vulnerable to grow. Defending themselves will undoubtedly be no small task.
Qu’importe. En plus d’intervenir sur le: No matter. In addition to working on housing, the committee also intends to roll up its sleeves on land-use planning issues. The “p'tit gars de Saint-Michel” (Saint-Michel's own kid), as he often introduces himself, likes to remind people that nothing is impossible, as shown by <l1>the recent victorious citizen mobilization against the developer Mondev</l1>. There is also the one under way to convert <l2>the former Francon quarry</l2> into a place for living and greenery that reflects the neighbourhood. “There's Frédéric-Bach Park: sure, it's beautiful, but excuse me, it's a park made for white people from Rosemont and Ahuntsic, it's not for us at all,” exclaims the man who nonetheless counts himself among the most privileged in the neighbourhood that watched him grow up.
Des mobilisations comme celles-là, il y: There will be more mobilizations like these.
Dès janvier 2024, le comité sera en mesu: Starting in January 2024, the committee will be able to offer volunteer services to Saint-Michel residents. With no premises of its own, because of the scarcity of available community spaces in the neighbourhood, it will initially be housed in another space or operate as a mobile clinic. Finally, the organization would like to make its activities sustainable by finding funds to hire staff, among other things.
« On aimerait être une réussite collecti: “We'd like to be a collective success. Personally, I'd like it to be a place of possibilities and victories, and I'd like to change the story of what happens in Saint-Michel. But also, and above all, to change people's destinies and their living conditions. We'll be able to tell ourselves that there are small revolutions on a human scale, and that they do exist,” hopes the lifelong Saint-Michel resident.
Selon l’Observatoire du Grand Montréal,: According to the Observatoire du Grand Montréal, <l1>the metropolis and its agglomeration are home to 53 per cent of Quebec's tenant households</l1>. In Saint-Michel, <l2>79 per cent of households were tenants in 2020, and more than a third devoted a high share of their income to rent</l2>. In the midst of a housing crisis, demands are pouring in from everywhere, and a groundswell of opposition is surfacing in every corner of the island… or almost.
Rares sont les quartiers montréalais qui: Few Montréal neighbourhoods lack a housing committee or a tenants' association. In disadvantaged areas like Montréal-Nord and Parc-Extension, residents can count on a structure to support them. But until very recently, Saint-Michel remained the poor cousin of tenant advocacy.
Pour Dominique Perreault, directrice de: For Dominique Perreault, director of the neighbourhood roundtable Vivre Saint-Michel en santé (VSMS), it is hard to explain why. “Having devoted 10 years to housing issues in another neighbourhood, I know Saint-Michel has always been a bit behind on this front. I imagine it goes back to a time when people thought it wasn't necessary to organize. Saint-Michel is a neighbourhood where rents were cheaper to begin with. Maybe there were also fewer problems to deal with, although they were probably hidden,” she tries to analyze cautiously. She also acknowledges that the difficulty of securing funding to create such organizations can discourage even the most determined.
Il y a pourtant eu, il y a près de 20 an: Yet nearly 20 years ago, there was the Bureau Info-Logement (BIL). Andres Barahona, a community organizer at the Centre éducatif communautaire René-Goupil, was there at the project's genesis. “Back then, residents mostly complained about unsanitary housing and abuse by landlords. But there was nothing in the neighbourhood [to support them],” he explains. The BIL came to address these concerns, while informing tenants of their rights and obligations. “There were immigrants who didn't dare complain, for fear of jeopardizing their status, and many people were afraid to speak out. (...) Quite frankly, going around visiting apartments, I saw things that made me wonder whether we were still in Quebec…” exclaims the community organizer, raising his eyebrows.
Le temps passe, mais les problèmes recen: Time passes, but the problems identified persist and worsen. The BIL was quickly overwhelmed with requests, the funds it received ran out, and recruitment suffered. “A few years ago, we had to put all of it on hold,” regrets Mr. Barahona. The BIL has since resumed its popular education and tenant support activities. Today, it welcomes the arrival of a housing committee. The neighbourhood of more than 56,000 residents indeed covers a very large territory. “Alongside us, the committee will be able to do mobilization and advocacy. We don't want a monopoly, especially in a neighbourhood like Saint-Michel, where needs are enormous. So it's a good thing there's a housing committee. We want to work in partnership so we can be complementary and better serve the population.”
Ancienne chargée de projet à VSMS, Yasmi: A former project manager at VSMS, Yasmine Belam accompanied and advised the founding members of the Comité Logement Citoyen. Above all, she was a privileged witness to their struggle. The UQAM doctoral candidate in sociology acknowledges that they are dedicated people, determined to shed light on Saint-Michel's housing needs. But residents, young people, immigrants, people in precarious situations and allies, everyone who makes up the neighbourhood, will need to come to their aid.
« Je pense que le milieu communautaire d: “I think the community sector needs to rethink its role. Historically, in Quebec and in Montréal, the community sector has been very political, but it has also taken on the tradition of being about service – as we see more of in Saint-Michel – rather than betting on people's power to act, putting them at the forefront and making their voices heard. (...) People need to be able to see themselves in their leaders and feel concerned. I believe there's something to deconstruct on that front,” insists the doctoral student.
Toutefois, elle se félicite de voir que: She is nonetheless pleased to see that several milestones have already been set in this regard. “We see many people who grew up in Saint-Michel coming back and getting involved,” explains the woman who lived in the neighbourhood when she was younger. Whether through <l1>Forward Movements</l1>, the Clinique juridique de Saint-Michel (CSJM) or the FJSM, which she cites as an example, Yasmine Belam believes it is Saint-Michel's youth who will turn the tide.
Mais comment grossir les rangs de la mob: But how can the ranks of the housing mobilization be swelled? To the west of Saint-Michel, in Parc-Extension, a neighbourhood facing similar issues, where the housing committee has existed for 30 years, people have often asked themselves this question and have since found a few answers.
Amy Darwich est coordonnatrice du Comité: Amy Darwich is coordinator of the Comité d'action de Parc-Extension (CAPE). “People tend to assume that because someone lives in a precarious situation, they won't want to get involved. That's not what we've found. On the contrary, we notice that it's people in precarious situations who mobilize the most, because they are the ones most affected by housing issues, or because they fear being forced to leave the neighbourhood (…) I think people get more involved when the issue is important,” says the coordinator.
« Il y aussi le fait que les espaces d’o: “There's also the fact that community organizing spaces are often monopolized by professionals and more seasoned activists, to the detriment of the people affected. So we have to find a way to include people and tell them they matter.” For example, all of CAPE's information materials are available in at least nine languages, all spoken in the neighbourhood. “We're also careful to have team members who represent the worst-housed people in the neighbourhood and who speak the languages of the communities that live here.” In fact, points out M<sup>s.</sup> Darwich, being able to build relationships based on trust remains essential to collective action.
Ces réflexions, le Comité Logement Citoy: The Comité Logement Citoyen Saint-Michel already has these reflections in mind. In the years to come, and once the organization has gained strength, the aim is to see only people who live in the neighbourhood sitting on its board of directors. Although Saint-Michel residents are currently members of the board, so are founders of the committee – mostly community workers – for the time it takes to consolidate the organization's foundations.
« On veut que le comité soit une figure: “We want the committee to be a figurehead, alongside other organizations, and to become a meeting place for residents and citizens who are struggling but want to get involved. Yes, we want to improve living conditions, but we're not going to turn Saint-Michel into Westmount overnight either. And that comes through building a sense of living together and a sense of belonging to the neighbourhood. We want to keep our people,”, says Alexandre Boucher Bonneau emphatically.
Retour au Café Saint-Mich. Juste en face: Back at Café Saint-Mich. Just across the street, a passerby is waiting for the bus. Has she heard of the brand-new housing committee? She isn't aware of it and doesn't know this kind of structure. Once informed, our interlocutor, who is a homeowner, is pleased about the committee's arrival: it could benefit a dear friend of hers who is having trouble finding an apartment.
Tout reste à faire. Mais certains signes: Everything remains to be done. But some signs suggest that the committee will be able to rally the Saint-Michel community from all walks of life.
